rows.description: A child lines up which toy to tidy first or which drawing to finish before dinner, picking by what feels most urgent or fun. Ordering things is new, so the plan changes the moment something shinier appears.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 7–12, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A schoolchild decides to play first and study later, sincerely believing there will be time. Working out that the hard, boring task should sometimes go first is a slowly learned skill, usually taught by a bad evening.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 4–6, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A teenager answers every message and does small chores while the big exam revision keeps sliding. Urgent things feel productive and loud, while important things are quiet and easy to postpone.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 4–6, 7–12, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A college student with assignments, placement prep, friends and family calls treats all of them as equally pressing and ends up doing none well. Ranking means accepting that something will be left undone.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 23–26

rows.subtype: Saying no to protect the main goal [Actor]
rows.description: A young professional declines a low-value request so a deadline-critical task gets protected time. It feels slightly rude and guilt-inducing, yet it is what keeps the important work from being crowded out.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 18–22

rows.description: A wise planner picks the three outcomes that matter most for the week, writes them down and checks them each evening. Short lists survive contact with real days; long lists just become guilt.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 18–22

rows.subtype: Big task feels like a wall [Actor]
rows.description: A child looking at a full chapter or a project chart sees only its size and freezes or wanders off. Without a first small piece in view, the task feels impossible rather than merely long.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 13–17, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A teenager writes study more as a plan and then sits with no idea where to begin. A goal without a first physical action such as solving five sums from chapter three leaves the mind with nothing to grip.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 7–12, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A student spends hours building a colour-coded schedule and feels progress without doing any of the work. Planning gives the comfort of action while the frightening first step stays untouched.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 7–12, 13–17, 23–26

rows.subtype: Splitting a project into checkable pieces [Response]
rows.description: A wise worker divides a large task into pieces that can each be finished in under an hour and ticks them off. Each completed piece gives real evidence of progress and lowers the dread of the whole.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 7–12, 13–17, 23–26
